body:
Risk retention and risk transfer

A government or household facing disaster risk must decide how potential financial losses will be managed. The 2 broad approaches are risk retention and risk transfer.

Under risk retention, the exposed person, business or government bears the financial consequences using its own resources or financing arrangements. Budgetary reserves and disaster funds are examples of planned retention. Borrowing provides finance, but the borrower remains responsible for repayment.

Under risk transfer, another party agrees, under specified conditions, to bear an agreed part of the financial risk. Insurance, reinsurance and catastrophe bonds can provide forms of risk transfer.

Insurance is a contractual arrangement in which an insurer accepts specified risks in return for a premium and pays according to the policy's terms when a covered event or condition occurs.

Insurance transfers specified financial risk, not the physical hazard itself. It does not prevent damage, and it does not necessarily reimburse every loss. Coverage limits, exclusions, deductibles and the definition of insured events matter.

Indemnity insurance and parametric insurance

FeatureIndemnity insuranceParametric insurance
Basis of paymentVerified covered loss under the policy.A predefined measurable trigger.
ExamplePayment for assessed damage to insured property.Payment when an agreed rainfall or wind-speed threshold is met.
AssessmentUsually requires assessment of the insured loss.Focuses on verifying the specified trigger.
Principal limitationClaims assessment can require time and documentation.Payment may differ from the actual loss suffered.

A parametric trigger is an agreed measurable condition, such as rainfall exceeding a specified threshold at defined locations during an agreed period. When the trigger is satisfied, payment is determined by the contract rather than by a separate assessment of each insured loss.

This can provide faster access to funds. However, it creates basis risk: actual damage and the index-based payout may not match. A village may suffer serious local flooding without the specified rainfall threshold being reached at the reference measuring station. In that case, a policy based solely on that trigger may not pay.

Parametric insurance does not guarantee payment whenever a disaster causes damage. The contract's specified trigger must be satisfied. A large actual loss may occur without a payout, while a triggered payout may differ from the amount of actual loss.

Catastrophe bonds

A catastrophe bond, often called a cat bond, is a financial instrument that transfers specified catastrophe risk to investors in capital markets.

Under a typical arrangement, investors provide capital and receive a return for accepting catastrophe risk. If the contractually specified catastrophic event or loss condition occurs, some or all of the capital at risk can be used to make a payment for disaster protection. If no qualifying event occurs during the bond's term, the principal is generally returned according to the bond's conditions.

Catastrophe bonds may use different trigger structures, including parametric or loss-based triggers. Their precise terms determine when investors bear losses and when the protected party receives funds.

Catastrophe bonds differ from ordinary borrowing. In ordinary borrowing, the borrower is generally obliged to repay the principal under the loan or bond terms. In a catastrophe bond, investors explicitly accept the possibility of losing agreed capital if the disaster trigger is met.

Contingent credit is not insurance

Contingent credit is finance arranged before a crisis that becomes accessible when agreed conditions are satisfied. It can help governments obtain liquidity rapidly after a disaster.

However, contingent credit is still a form of borrowing. Unless a separate contractual provision says otherwise, the borrower must repay it. It should therefore be distinguished from an insurance payment or risk transfer through a catastrophe bond.

Disaster risk layering

Risk layering means using different financing instruments for different levels of disaster frequency and severity. The purpose is to avoid relying on a single instrument for every possible event.

Smaller, more frequent losses may be managed through predictable budgetary resources and reserves. Larger shocks may require pre-arranged credit. Rare, severe losses may justify insurance, reinsurance or catastrophe bonds, subject to affordability and availability.

This arrangement is illustrative rather than compulsory. The suitable combination depends on local hazards, expected losses, fiscal capacity, insurance-market conditions and the cost of each instrument.

An Indian example of parametric insurance

The Sixteenth Finance Commission's Report for 2026–31 describes Nagaland's Disaster Risk Transfer Parametric Insurance Solution as an Indian example of State-level disaster risk transfer for extreme rainfall. The arrangement uses defined rainfall-related triggers rather than relying solely on post-event assessment of individual physical losses.

The report also recommends further examination of innovative insurance products and catastrophe bonds. A recommendation to study an instrument is not evidence that every State has adopted it.

Prelims focus

  • Risk retention: the exposed entity bears the financial consequences.
  • Risk transfer: specified financial risk is transferred to another party.
  • Indemnity insurance: payment is linked to verified covered loss.
  • Parametric insurance: payment depends on an agreed measurable trigger.
  • Basis risk: the mismatch between actual loss and index-based payment.
  • Trap: Contingent credit is repayable borrowing, whereas a catastrophe bond can place agreed catastrophe losses on investors.

[Sources: World Bank, Disaster Risk Finance and Insurance, overview and risk-layering approach; World Bank Treasury, Disaster Risk Management, sections Catastrophe Bonds, Insurance and Reinsurance, and Derivatives; World Bank, Managing Flood Risks: Leveraging Finance for Business Resilience in Malaysia, discussion of parametric insurance and basis risk, printed p. 104; Sixteenth Finance Commission, Report for 2026–31, Volume I, chapter 11, paragraphs 11.88–11.91, printed pp. 250–252. Online sources consulted 2 November 2026.]

pictures.caption: Different financing instruments are suited to different layers of disaster risk.

title: Insurance, Catastrophe Bonds and Disaster Risk Transfer

body:
Why financial recovery must include vulnerable households

A disaster can reduce household earnings while increasing expenditure on food, shelter, transport, healthcare and repairs. Families with limited savings may borrow at high cost, sell livestock or work equipment, withdraw children from school or postpone essential healthcare.

These coping actions may help a family meet immediate needs but can weaken its ability to recover over the longer term. For this reason, social protection is an important part of disaster recovery.

Social protection refers to public policies and programmes intended to protect people against poverty, vulnerability and economic insecurity. In disaster recovery, it can help affected households maintain essential consumption and restore livelihoods.

Shock-responsive or adaptive social protection

Shock-responsive social protection adjusts social assistance systems when a major disaster or other shock increases people's needs. It can use existing programmes, administrative capacity and delivery systems to reach affected households.

There are 2 important forms of expansion.

ExpansionWhat changes?Example
Vertical expansionThe value or duration of support for existing beneficiaries increases.An existing eligible household receives an additional temporary cash transfer after a flood.
Horizontal expansionMore people or households become covered.Newly affected households receive temporary assistance even though they were not regular beneficiaries.

Vertical expansion changes the depth of support for existing beneficiaries. Horizontal expansion changes the number of people covered. A programme may combine both approaches.

Other measures can include temporary employment, public works, food support or assistance to restart productive activities. Their suitability depends on the disaster's effects, existing programmes and available administrative capacity.

Social protection is not the same as insurance

Insurance payments arise from the terms of an insurance contract. Social assistance is provided through public programmes and eligibility rules. A household may receive social protection even if it has no insurance policy.

Similarly, the purpose of a temporary social transfer may be to prevent hunger, distress sales or severe hardship rather than to reimburse the full monetary value of destroyed property.

Fiscal resilience of government

Fiscal resilience is the ability of government finances to absorb and manage shocks while maintaining essential public services and sustainable financial commitments.

A government may suffer from 2 simultaneous pressures after a disaster: expenditure increases because response and reconstruction are required, while revenue may decline because economic activity has slowed.

Fiscal resilience can be strengthened through:

  • Risk reduction: preventing avoidable damage reduces future financial pressure.
  • Prepared budgets and funds: improving the availability of money for urgent expenditure.
  • Appropriate risk transfer: obtaining protection against selected severe financial losses.
  • Prudent borrowing: meeting financing needs without creating unsustainable repayment burdens.
  • Social protection: helping vulnerable households recover without destructive coping measures.
  • Accountability: recording expenditure, monitoring recovery works and checking whether assistance reaches intended beneficiaries.

Connecting assessment, finance and Build Back Better

Effective recovery requires 3 questions to be answered together: What was affected? What must be restored or improved? How will the necessary work be financed?

Damage-and-loss assessment identifies physical and economic effects. Recovery planning converts the findings into prioritised needs. Public funds, insurance and other financing instruments provide resources. Social protection helps households maintain well-being and restore earnings. Risk reduction ensures that reconstruction does not recreate the same vulnerabilities.

A good recovery programme is therefore judged not only by money spent or buildings completed, but also by whether essential services function, livelihoods return, vulnerable groups receive suitable assistance and the community becomes better prepared for future disasters.

Public accountability and recovery outcomes

Transparent records of damage, expenditure, completed works and beneficiary assistance allow authorities to compare planned activities with actual results. Grievance mechanisms help affected people report exclusion, delays or other problems.

Monitoring should distinguish financial progress from recovery outcomes. Releasing a grant does not by itself prove that a family has regained safe housing. Constructing a health facility does not by itself prove that healthcare has become accessible. These differences matter when assessing whether recovery has genuinely succeeded.

Prelims focus

  • Vertical expansion: more support for existing social-protection beneficiaries.
  • Horizontal expansion: coverage extended to additional beneficiaries.
  • Social protection can support households without requiring an insurance contract.
  • Fiscal resilience involves managing disaster-related financial shocks while maintaining essential government functions.
  • Effective recovery combines assessment, financing, livelihood restoration and risk reduction.
  • Trap: Expenditure or grant disbursement alone does not prove that recovery outcomes have been achieved.

[Sources: World Bank, How the World Bank Supports Shock-Responsive Social Protection Systems, explanation of horizontal and vertical expansion (24 May 2022); World Bank, Crisis and Disaster Risk Finance: Short Notes on COVID-19, section on adaptive social protection and disaster risk finance (2020); NCERT, Introductory Macroeconomics, Class 12, chapter 5, Government Budget and the Economy, sections 5.1–5.2, reprint 2026–27; UNDP, Post-Disaster Needs Assessment, recovery-planning framework (2015); UNDRR, Sendai Framework for Disaster Risk Reduction 2015–2030, Priority 4. Online sources consulted 2 November 2026.]
